title: Species-agnostic tools for Influenza A H5 antibody and NP antigen detection in dairy cows, chickens, and humans
abstract: High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza (HPAI) A (H5N1) circulates in wild birds, causing outbreaks in domestic poultry, but recently became enzootic in the United States spilling over into various mammals, including cattle. The zoonotic potential of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b emphasizes the need for tools for surveillance in mammalian and avian species. We developed two species-agnostic assays using the Meso Scale Discovery (MSD) platform to enhance current surveillance methods: a sandwich immunoassay for influenza A nucleoprotein (NP) antigen, and a bridging serology assay for influenza A/H5 specific antibodies. We assessed the assays by testing milk and serum from cattle herds experiencing H5N1 incursions, serum from H5N1-vaccinated humans and chickens, and negative control samples from cattle, chickens, and humans. Antibodies and antigen were detected in milk and serum from H5-exposed cattle herds, but not in samples from putatively naïve herds. The number of identified exposed animals increased by combining antigen and antibody testing. The bridging serology assay accurately differentiated serum from H5-vaccinated chickens and humans, relative to H5-naïve controls. abstract_zh: 高致病性 禽流感 (HPAI) A (H5N1) 在 野生鸟类 中传播,在家禽中引起 暴发,但最近在美国成为地方性流行病,并蔓延到包括牛在内的各种哺乳动物中。H5N1 进化枝 2.3.4.4b 的人畜共患潜力强调了在哺乳动物和鸟类物种中需要 监测 工具。我们使用 Meso Scale Discovery (MSD) 平台开发了两种与物种无关的测定法,以增强当前的 监测 方法:针对甲型流感核蛋白 (NP) 抗原的夹心免疫测定法,以及针对甲型流感/H5 特异性抗体的桥接 血清学 测定法。我们通过测试来自经历 H5N1 入侵的牛群的牛奶和血清、来自接种 H5N1 疫苗的人类和鸡的血清以及来自牛、鸡和人类的阴性对照样本来评估检测结果。在暴露于 H5 的牛群的牛奶和血清中检测到了抗体和抗原,但在假定的未接触牛群的样本中未检测到抗体和抗原。通过结合抗原和抗体测试,增加了确定的暴露动物的数量。相对于未接种 H5 的对照,桥接 血清学 测定可准确地区分 H5 疫苗接种鸡和人的血清。使用 H1 血凝素封闭可减少潜在的交叉反应,从而改善了 H5 疫苗接种者样本和假定阴性人类样本之间的区分。这些研究证明了这些方法对不同物种的适用性,并促进它们在 监测 研究中的使用。

title: Comparative Evaluation of Lipid Nanoparticles for Influenza mRNA Vaccines: Immunogenicity and Cross-Reactive Immune Responses
abstract: Influenza remains a significant global public health concern due to seasonal epidemics, continuous antigenic evolution, and the potential emergence of highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses. Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines offer a flexible platform for rapid vaccine development; however, the influence of lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations on vaccine-induced immunogenicity and cross-protective responses remains insufficiently understood. This preclinical study aims to compare the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of influenza mRNA vaccines formulated with three different LNPs: ALC-0315, SM-102, and the novel SX-104 formulation. Using BALB/c mouse models, quadrivalent mRNA vaccines encoding haemagglutinin (HA) antigens from seasonal influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata strains will be evaluated. The impact of pre-existing immunity on vaccine responses will also be investigated. Humoral immune responses will be assessed using microneutralization assays, while cellular immune responses will be characterized through intracellular cytokine staining and flow cytometry to evaluate antigen-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell responses. Cross-reactive immunity will be investigated against antigenically distinct H1N1 and H3N2 strains, including T-cell responses targeting conserved HA regions. Furthermore, animal challenge studies will assess protective efficacy against influenza infection and investigate the contributions of humoral and cellular immunity to vaccine-mediated protection. The potential cross-protective effects against highly pathogenic avian influenza H5 and H7 viruses will also be evaluated. The findings are expected to provide insights into how different LNP formulations influence the magnitude and breadth of influenza vaccine-induced immune responses, supporting the optimization of mRNA vaccine formulations and the development of broader influenza vaccination strategies.

title: Bioinspired Membrane Fusion–Gated Hydrogel Biosensor for Extraction‐Free Viral RNA Detection of Infectious Influenza Virus
abstract: Emerging infectious diseases driven by zoonotic spillover demand rapid and reliable molecular diagnostics for pathogen identification and surveillance. However, conventional nucleic acid diagnostics cannot distinguish infectious virions from nonviable RNA fragments, limiting infectivity-resolved virus identification. Here, we report a bioinspired membrane-coated hydrogel (Memgel) sensor that enables extraction-free molecular detection of influenza virus while distinguishing fusion-competent virions from noninfectious viral material. The platform integrates a cell-mimetic supported lipid bilayer with a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) hydrogel matrix encapsulating recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) reagents. Under endosome-mimicking acidic conditions, hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion selectively delivers viral genomic RNA from infectious virions into the hydrogel matrix, triggering sequence-specific amplification while suppressing signals from free viral RNA fragments. As a proof of concept, the Memgel sensor was evaluated for the detection of influenza A (H9N2) in simulated nasal fluid and raw milk matrices, achieving a limit of detection of 10 1.23 TCID 50 mL - 1 while maintaining robust detection performance without RNA extraction. Coupled with a portable fluorescence reader, the system demonstrates compatibility with compact fluorescence-based readout for future point-of-care implementation. This fusion-gated sensing strategy provides a materials-based framework for infectivity-resolved molecular diagnostics of emerging viral pathogens.

abstract_zh: 由人畜共患 跨物种溢出 驱动的新发传染病需要快速可靠的分子诊断来进行病原体识别和 监测。然而,传统的核酸诊断无法区分感染性病毒粒子和非活性RNA片段,限制了感染性解决的病毒识别。在这里,我们报告了一种仿生膜涂层水凝胶(Memgel)传感器,它能够实现流感病毒的免提取分子检测,同时区分具有融合能力的病毒粒子和非感染性病毒材料。该平台将细胞模拟支持的脂质双层与封装重组酶聚合酶扩增(RPA)试剂的聚乙二醇二丙烯酸酯(PEGDA)水凝胶基质集成在一起。在模拟内体的酸性条件下,血凝素介导的膜融合选择性地将病毒基因组RNA从感染性病毒粒子递送到水凝胶基质中,触发序列特异性扩增,同时抑制来自游离病毒RNA片段的信号。作为概念验证,对 Memgel 传感器在模拟鼻液和原料奶基质中检测甲型流感 (H9N2) 的情况进行了评估,实现了 10 1.23 TCID 50 mL - 1 的检测限,同时在不提取 RNA 的情况下保持了稳健的检测性能。与便携式荧光读数器相结合,该系统展示了与基于荧光的紧凑型读数器的兼容性,以供未来的护理点实施。这种融合门控传感策略为新兴病毒病原体的感染性解析分子诊断提供了基于材料的框架。

title: Come together: Coordinate deconvolution of viral recombination, reassortment, and epistatic survival
abstract: Viral subtyping and recombination detection underpin taxonomic curation, clinical resistance tracking, and real-time outbreak surveillance. Community nomenclature systems—such as HIV-1 circulating recombinant forms (CRFs), SARS-CoV-2 Pango lineages, and Influenza A genotype catalogs—have created indispensable shared vocabularies, yet rapid archive growth and frequent cross-lineage chimerism now invite a complementary layer that unites speed, provenance, and statistical rigor across viral families. Here, we present EGGMAN (Exact Genomic Genealogy and Mosaic Ancestry Nomenclature), a unified framework that separates mapping physical parental coordinates against a principled, non-mosaic founder basis (Tier 1) from statistically guarded assignment to established epidemic clones (Tier 2). By combining reference-free recombination scrubbing (RhizAeon), emergence-anchored founder rooting (ChronAeon), and portable pathogen specifications, one engine processes contiguous genomes (HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2, wildlife sarbecoviruses) and segmented reassortants (Influenza A) at thousands of sequences per second on a laptop or in a browser—preserving legacy clade names while giving emerging chimeras transparent, coordinate-based identifiers on Day 1. Across public surveillance archives, EGGMAN harmonizes the HIV-1 reference catalog and genealogy, reconciles >120,000 clinical pol records in Stanford HIVDB, separates emerging CRFs and a monophyletic regional lineage from convergent recombination hotspots, and tracks unannotated H5Nx reassortants and SARS-CoV-2 X* waves without temporal lookahead. Finally, census-level mapping across 761 HIV-1 mosaic lineages reveals a two-stage selective sieve separating within-host protein-folding viability (gp120 and Gag-CA cores) from between-host preservation of an intact 3' regulatory and envelope cassette.

abstract_zh: 病毒亚型和重组检测支撑分类学管理、临床耐药性跟踪和实时 暴发 监测。社区命名系统——例如 HIV-1 循环重组形式 (CRF)、SARS-CoV-2 Pango 谱系和甲型流感基因型目录——已经创建了不可或缺的共享词汇表,但快速的档案增长和频繁的跨谱系嵌合现象现在引入了一个补充层,将跨病毒家族的速度、来源和统计严谨性统一起来。在这里,我们提出了 EGGMAN(精确基因组谱系和马赛克祖先命名法),这是一个统一的框架,它将根据有原则的非马赛克创始人基础(第 1 层)映射物理亲本坐标与已建立的流行克隆的统计保护分配(第 2 层)分开。通过结合无参考重组清理 (RhizAeon)、出现锚定的创始人生根 (ChronAeon) 和便携式病原体规范,一个引擎可以在笔记本电脑或浏览器中以每秒数千个序列处理连续的 基因组(HIV-1、SARS-CoV-2、野生动物 sarbecoviruses)和分段重配病毒(A 型流感),从而保留传统进化枝名称,同时赋予新兴嵌合体透明、第一天基于坐标的标识符。在公共 监测 档案中,EGGMAN 协调了 HIV-1 参考目录和谱系,协调了斯坦福 HIVDB 中超过 120,000 条临床 pol 记录,将新兴 CRF 和单系区域谱系与聚合重组热点分开,并在没有时间前瞻的情况下跟踪未注释的 H5Nx 重配体和 SARS-CoV-2 X* 波。最后,761 个 HIV-1 嵌合谱系的普查水平图谱揭示了一个两阶段选择性筛,将 宿主 内蛋白质折叠活力(gp120 和 Gag-CA 核心)与 宿主 间完整 3' 调控和包膜盒的保存分开。

title: Are we finally getting on top of influenza?
abstract: Seasonal influenza remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in older adults, but with United States Food and Drug Administration approval of mRNA vaccines for seasonal influenza for those over 50 years of age, we should see cases and deaths significantly reduced. Moderna’s mRNA-1010 has demonstrated superior efficacy to a standard-dose influenza vaccine while maintaining an acceptable safety profile. The platform offers important advantages, including rapid manufacture and more timely vaccine strain selection, which will result in improved protection against antigenic drift. mRNA technology may also enable combination vaccines targeting influenza, COVID-19 and other respiratory viruses. Together with emerging H5N1 mRNA vaccines, these developments will likely substantially improve influenza control and strengthen preparedness for future pandemic threats.

source_body_en: Seasonal influenza remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in older adults, but with United States Food and Drug Administration approval of mRNA vaccines for seasonal influenza for those over 50 years of age, we should see cases and deaths significantly reduced. Together with emerging H5N1 mRNA vaccines, these developments will likely substantially improve influenza control and strengthen preparedness for future pandemic threats.

title: Genetic characterization of swine influenza A viruses, including a putative reassortant strain, in Finland, 2014-2025.
abstract: Swine influenza A viruses (swIAV) are capable of reassortment, which can lead to the emergence of novel strains with pandemic potential. In this study, we determined whole-genome sequences of 38 clinical swIAV strains circulating in Finland in 2014-2025. All strains were identified as the H1N1 subtype and further classified into three distinct H1 HA clades: two avian-like clades H1C.2.1 (n = 28) and H1C.2.4 (n = 6), and the pandemic clade H1A.3.3.2 (n = 4). Phylogenetic analysis of all eight gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, NA, HA, MP, NP and NS) identified a strain, comprising an HA gene derived from the H1C.2.4 clade, while the remaining seven genes originated from the H1C.2.1 clade, suggesting a reassortment event. This study contributes to expanding the genetic database of influenza A viruses in pigs and reveals the genetic characteristics and evolution of swIAV in Finland, a relatively isolated swine production system with limited international movement of live pigs.

title: The evolution and transmission dynamics of H3N2 influenza virus identified in a respiratory disease outbreak in companion dogs in Alabama, USA
abstract: H3N2 Canine influenza virus (CIV)​, initially of avian origin, emerged in Asia around 2005–2007 and subsequently spread globally, reaching the USA in 2015. Despite initial containment efforts, H3N2 CIV re-emerged in several USA states in 2023. This study investigates the evolution and transmission dynamics of H3N2 CIV identified in companion dogs during an outbreak in Alabama, USA, between August and October 2022. We performed whole-genome sequencing on five H3N2 CIV isolates and conducted phylodynamic modeling, incorporating 100 global H3N2 CIV genomes per segment. Phylogenetic reconstruction showed the Alabama strains formed distinct, tightly clustered groups, suggesting recent common ancestry and localized evolution. Phylogeographic inference revealed discordant origins for different gene segments. The Hemagglutinin (HA), Matrix Protein (MP), Nucleoprotein (NP), Non-structural Protein (NS),​ and Polymerase Acidic (PA) genes traced ancestry to California strains, the Neuraminidase (NA) gene to Florida strains, and the Polymerase Basic1 (PB1) and Polymerase Basic2 (PB2) genes to Illinois strains. This genomic incongruence strongly indicates that the Alabama outbreak strain emerged through a reassortment event involving viruses from these three geographically distinct regions. The findings highlight reassortment as a mechanism driving H3N2 CIV evolution and spread, likely facilitated by the movement of infected dogs. Low vaccination coverage in dogs requires continued surveillance and shelter-focused vaccination to control CIV outbreaks and monitor adaptation.

title: Characteristics of emergency health systems guidance: an evaluation using AGREE-HS tool
abstract: Objective Based on the Appraisal of Guidelines Research & Evaluation – Health Systems (AGREE-HS) tool, this study aimed to conduct a demonstrative evaluation of selected emergency health systems guidance (HSG) documents developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), in order to summarize and explore their development characteristics. Methods We searched the WHO IRIS database (inception to May 20, 2024) for documents on COVID-19, EVD, MERS, H1N1, H7N9, and SARS. After screening, six trained appraisers in three pairs showed consistency (all ICC (2,1) >0.75). Included documents were scored with the AGREE-HS five items (35 criteria), and overall and item-specific scores were compared among diseases. Results 136 emergency HSGs were included (COVID-19101, EVD 13, H1N1 9, MERS 6, SARS 7; none for H7N9). The pilot ICCs among the three appraisal pairs were 0.824 (95% CI: 0.343–0.978), 0.814 (95% CI: 0.395–0.976), and 0.828 (95% CI: 0.448–0.978), indicating good agreement. Overall scores ranged from 31.67%–85.00% (mean 59.07 ± 11.76%). Mean item scores: Topic 5.22, Recommendations 5.15, Implementability 4.32, Methods 4.24, Participants 3.79. COVID-19 scored highest overall (61.16%), higher than EVD (52.44%, p Recommendations > Implementability > Methods > Participants, with MERS and SARS lowest in Participants and Implementability. After Bonferroni correction, significant differences remained only for Recommendations (SARS vs. H1N1, p < 0.05; EVD vs. COVID-19, p < 0.05; SARS vs. COVID-19, p < 0.001) and Implementability (SARS vs. COVID-19, p < 0.05); no other item showed significant between-group differences. Appraisers noted strengths in topic focus and recommendation clarity but weaknesses in competing interest management, evidence review transparency, and implementation strategies. Conclusion Emergency HSG prioritizes targeted topic and practical recommendations, optimizing resource allocation and research methods while ensuring implementability. Although description of competing interests and funding management is simplified, these documents demonstrate disciplinary breadth and transparency. High-quality emergency guidance requires balancing rigorous evidence assessment, multidisciplinary collaboration, and resource coordination to build an efficient, sustainable response system.

title_zh: 紧急卫生系统指导的特点:使用 AGREE-HS 工具进行评估
source_body_en: Objective Based on the Appraisal of Guidelines Research & Evaluation – Health Systems (AGREE-HS) tool, this study aimed to conduct a demonstrative evaluation of selected emergency health systems guidance (HSG) documents developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), in order to summarize and explore their development characteristics. Methods We searched the WHO IRIS database (inception to May 20, 2024) for documents on COVID-19, EVD, MERS, H1N1, H7N9, and SARS. After screening, six trained appraisers in three pairs showed consistency (all ICC (2,1) >0.75). Included documents were scored with the AGREE-HS five items (35 criteria), and overall and item-specific scores were compared among diseases. Results 136 emergency HSGs were included (COVID-19101, EVD 13, H1N1 9, MERS 6, SARS 7; none for H7N9). The pilot ICCs among the three appraisal pairs were 0.824 (95% CI: 0.343–0.978), 0.814 (95% CI: 0.395–0.976), and 0.828 (95% CI: 0.448–0.978), indicating good agreement. Overall scores ranged from 31.67%–85.00% (mean 59.07 ± 11.76%). Mean item scores: Topic 5.22, Recommendations 5.15, Implementability 4.32, Methods 4.24, Participants 3.79. COVID-19 scored highest overall (61.16%), higher than EVD (52.44%, p Recommendations > Implementability > Methods > Participants, with MERS and SARS lowest in Participants and Implementability. After Bonferroni correction, significant differences remained only for Recommendations (SARS vs. H1N1, p < 0.05; EVD vs. COVID-19, p < 0.05; SARS vs. COVID-19, p < 0.001) and Implementability (SARS vs. COVID-19, p < 0.05); no other item showed significant between-group differences. Appraisers noted strengths in topic focus and recommendation clarity but weaknesses in competing interest management, evidence review transparency, and implementation strategies. Conclusion Emergency HSG prioritizes targeted topic and practical recommendations, optimizing resource allocation and research methods while ensuring implementability. Although description of competing interests and funding management is simplified, these documents demonstrate disciplinary breadth and transparency. High-quality emergency guidance requires balancing rigorous evidence assessment, multidisciplinary collaboration, and resource coordination to build an efficient, sustainable response system.

title: Quantifying Viscoelastic Alterations in Virus-Infected Cells by Optical Tweezers.
abstract: The viscoelasticity of cells is closely related to their physiological functions, influencing processes such as differentiation, proliferation, and migration. Viruses replicate by infecting host cells and can affect the cells' viscoelastic properties. However, current research mainly focuses on changes in the overall cellular viscoelasticity, while intracellular viscoelastic properties remain difficult to measure. Optical tweezers, due to their noncontact nature, offer a promising tool for measuring intracellular viscoelasticity. In this study, the viscoelastic moduli of host cells infected with three different viruses (H9N2, PRV, and HSV) were measured using the active-passive calibration method and microrheological techniques. The changes in viscoelastic moduli across different frequency ranges were systematically analyzed. The results showed that viral infection altered the viscoelastic properties of cells, with the extent of changes varying by virus type. We conclude that viral infection leads to an increase in viscous modulus and a decrease in elastic modulus of the host cell, and this is attributed to virus-induced depolymerization of the cytoskeleton, which reduces cellular elasticity and increases viscosity. These findings provide insights into the mechanisms of virus-induced alterations in cellular viscoelasticity and offer a theoretical foundation for further studies on the cellular mechanisms of viral infections.

full_text: The arrival of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b on mainland Australia in June 2026 represents more than the loss of one of the last major geographic barriers to the current panzootic. It illustrates the capacity of this virus to exploit interconnected wildlife populations across continents and oceans. The first confirmed mainland detection occurred in a migratory brown skua ( Stercorarius antarcticus ) near Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia, followed by detection in a southern giant petrel. Genomic analyses indicate that these viruses were most closely related to those circulating on Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean and suggest independent incursions from the sub‐Antarctic region rather than local transmission between the birds involved in the earliest detections [1, 2, 3].This finding marks another stage in the extraordinary intercontinental expansion of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. Viruses belonging to this clade spread from Europe to North America, reached South America in 2022, and subsequently expanded into sub‐Antarctic islands and Antarctica. Genomic analyses of viruses collected in Antarctica have placed them within South American H5N1 diversity and revealed multiple independent introductions into the Antarctic region [4, 5]. By October 2025, H5N1 had reached Heard Island, approximately 4000 km southwest of mainland Australia, before viruses closely related to those circulating there were detected in migratory seabirds in Western Australia in 2026 [2, 3]. Rather than representing an isolated Australian event, this incursion therefore constitutes the latest extension of an interconnected transmission network spanning the Americas, Antarctic and sub‐Antarctic ecosystems, and Oceania.What followed illustrates the consequences of viral incursion into interconnected wildlife communities. By 23 October 2026, Australia had recorded 722 confirmed H5 avian influenza events in wildlife across multiple jurisdictions. Detections were no longer restricted to migratory seabirds but involved resident birds, raptors, and waterbirds, as well as multiple mammalian species, including long‐nosed fur seals, Australian sea lions, dolphins, red foxes, and southern elephant seals [6, 7]. Importantly, detections across several mammalian species do not themselves demonstrate sustained mammal‐to‐mammal transmission, and genomic investigation remains essential to distinguish repeated avian‐to‐mammalian spillover events from transmission within mammalian populations. Nevertheless, the rapid expansion across host species following the initial seabird incursions illustrates how quickly a wildlife incursion can evolve into a multispecies One Health challenge.Australia had implemented targeted surveillance before the mainland incursion, testing hundreds of wild birds and Australian sea lions without detecting H5N1 [8]. The subsequent emergence of the virus therefore highlights an important distinction: surveillance can provide early warning, but the absence of detection cannot eliminate the risk posed by highly mobile wildlife populations across vast and incompletely sampled ecosystems. The relevant question is no longer whether surveillance should be intensified, but whether existing surveillance and biosecurity paradigms are sufficiently adapted to a virus circulating across wildlife, environmental, and production interfaces.Experience from other affected countries illustrates the limitations of relying on conventional farm‐level biosecurity alone. During the 2022–2023 H5N1 epidemic in Japan, commercial layer farms housing ≥ 100,000 birds were at increased risk of HPAI introduction, whereas basic biosecurity measures, including changing footwear at poultry‐house entrances, were associated with reduced risk [9]. These findings illustrate how farm structure and flock size can influence vulnerability to viral introduction and reinforce that biosecurity cannot be considered independently of production characteristics, human movement, and environmental exposure.Europe provides an equally important warning. During June–August 2026, HPAI A(H5N1) continued to circulate in wild birds across Europe, with 103 detections reported in 11 countries. Although only two poultry outbreaks were reported during this period, direct or indirect contact with wild birds remained the main source of HPAI virus introduction into domestic bird establishments [10]. This persistent wildlife‐to‐poultry interface highlights how repeated viral incursions can remain a major vulnerability even in regions with established surveillance and animal‐health infrastructure.These observations raise a broader question for global H5N1 governance. Current international frameworks appropriately emphasize outbreak notification, poultry biosecurity, surveillance, rapid response, and scientifically justified trade measures [1]. However, the contemporary ecology of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b extends far beyond a predominantly poultry‐centered model of disease control. Persistent circulation in wild birds, environmental contamination, long‐distance viral dispersal through migratory species, and recurrent spillover into terrestrial and marine mammals increasingly challenge approaches centered primarily on farms and recognized outbreaks. The continued global expansion of H5N1 therefore calls for international guidance to evolve beyond reactive outbreak management towards sustained management of interconnected wildlife‐environment‐livestock interfaces.Australia has an opportunity to incorporate these lessons before widespread poultry involvement occurs. As of 24 October 2026, no H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections had been detected in Australian poultry or humans, and the risk to the general population remained low [6, 11]. Preserving this separation will require more than replicating control systems developed elsewhere. Wildlife and environmental surveillance should be directly linked to risk‐based interventions in poultry, whereas genomic sequencing should be sufficiently rapid and representative to reconstruct introduction and transmission pathways. Farm biosecurity should account for production structure and environmental exposure rather than rely solely on standardized measures, and surveillance of occupationally exposed people should be integrated with animal‐health signals. For threatened wildlife, mortality surveillance should also be linked to population‐level ecological monitoring so that conservation impacts can be recognized before population declines become irreversible.Australia's H5N1 outbreak is therefore not simply a new national biosecurity emergency. It is the latest chapter in a panzootic that has progressively crossed geographic, ecological, and host barriers. Its expansion from the Americas through Antarctic and sub‐Antarctic ecosystems to Oceania illustrates why no country can regard H5N1 circulation in wildlife beyond its borders as an external problem. Experiences in Japan and Europe further show that established surveillance and farm biosecurity systems cannot eliminate the risk of repeated viral incursions. The challenge for Australia, and for international animal‐health governance, is therefore to move beyond preparedness frameworks focused primarily on detecting and containing outbreaks towards systems capable of anticipating viral movement across wildlife, environmental, agricultural, and human interfaces. Ultimately, the success of Australia's response should be measured not only by how rapidly H5N1 is detected but also by whether the lessons from this panzootic can prevent the next interface from being crossed. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study addresses the need to understand the spread of H5N1 avian influenza and its implications for global health, highlighting the virus's ability to expand beyond traditional geographic barriers.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes the detection of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in migratory birds across Australia, including a brown skua and a southern giant petrel, and traces its origin to Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean.
analysis.methods: Genomic analyses were conducted to determine the relationship between the detected viruses and those circulating in Heard Island, suggesting independent incursions rather than local transmission.
analysis.main_results: The first confirmed mainland detection of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in Australia was in a brown skua and a southern giant petrel, with genomic evidence indicating these viruses were most closely related to those on Heard Island.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate the virus's capacity to spread across continents and oceans through interconnected wildlife populations, marking a new stage in its intercontinental expansion.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides critical insights into the surveillance and preparedness needed for H5N1 avian influenza, emphasizing the importance of monitoring migratory bird populations for early detection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on genomic data from a small number of detected cases, but the evidence is strong due to the clear genetic relationship to viruses on Heard Island.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the spread of H5N1 avian influenza in Australia, highlighting the virus's ability to expand beyond traditional geographic barriers. The first confirmed mainland detection occurred in a brown skua and a southern giant petrel near Cape Le Grand National Park, with genomic analyses indicating these viruses were most closely related to those on Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean. The findings suggest independent incursions from the sub-Antarctic region rather than local transmission, marking another stage in the intercontinental expansion of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. The study underscores the need for enhanced surveillance of migratory bird populations to monitor and prepare for future outbreaks. While the study is limited by its reliance on a small number of cases, the genetic evidence supports the conclusion that the virus has outgrown conventional preparedness measures. These insights have significant implications for global health and wildlife disease monitoring.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study addresses the need to understand the spread of H5N1 avian influenza and its implications for global health, highlighting the virus's ability to expand beyond traditional geographic barriers.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study describes the detection of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in migratory birds across Australia, including a brown skua and a southern giant petrel, and traces its origin to Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean.
analysis_en.methods: Genomic analyses were conducted to determine the relationship between the detected viruses and those circulating in Heard Island, suggesting independent incursions rather than local transmission.
analysis_en.main_results: The first confirmed mainland detection of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in Australia was in a brown skua and a southern giant petrel, with genomic evidence indicating these viruses were most closely related to those on Heard Island.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate the virus's capacity to spread across continents and oceans through interconnected wildlife populations, marking a new stage in its intercontinental expansion.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides critical insights into the surveillance and preparedness needed for H5N1 avian influenza, emphasizing the importance of monitoring migratory bird populations for early detection.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on genomic data from a small number of detected cases, but the evidence is strong due to the clear genetic relationship to viruses on Heard Island.

source_body_en: Genomic analyses indicate that these viruses were most closely related to those circulating on Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean and suggest independent incursions from the sub‐Antarctic region rather than local transmission between the birds involved in the earliest detections [1, 2, 3].This finding marks another stage in the extraordinary intercontinental expansion of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. These findings illustrate how farm structure and flock size can influence vulnerability to viral introduction and reinforce that biosecurity cannot be considered independently of production characteristics, human movement, and environmental exposure.Europe provides an equally important warning. Author Contributions Md Jisan Ahmed: conceptualization, visualization, writing – original draft, writing – review and editing. Ritu Chalise: conceptualization, investigation, writing – original draft, writing – review and editing. Prajwal Bhandari: conceptualization, investigation, writing – review and editing, writing – original draft. The arrival of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b on mainland Australia in June 2026 represents more than the loss of one of the last major geographic barriers to the current panzootic. It illustrates the capacity of this virus to exploit interconnected wildlife populations across continents and oceans. The first confirmed mainland detection occurred in a migratory brown skua ( Stercorarius antarcticus ) near Cape Le Grand National Park in Western Australia, followed by detection in a southern giant petrel. Viruses belonging to this clade spread from Europe to North America, reached South America in 2022, and subsequently expanded into sub‐Antarctic islands and Antarctica. full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2357–2359 | 2357 Vaccine preparedness for the next emerging infectious disease crisis Florian Krammer Recent outbreaks with viruses such as Bundi­bugyo virus and Andes virus are a reminder that another pandemic can happen at any time. This Comment summarizes where we stand with pandemic preparedness from a vaccine perspective. During the COVID-19 pandemic, we witnessed vaccine develop­ment at its finest. Vaccines against the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed and were made available within approximately 1 year after the outbreak started1. This swift devel­ opment of vaccines was facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform2 but also by a wealth of exist­ ing knowledge because of many years of virology, vacci­nology and structural biology research. Much has happened since the COVID-19 pandemic. Technology has evolved, new insights into mechanisms of protection and basic immunology have been gained and regulatory and policy views have changed (Fig. 1), especially in the USA. Where does this leave us with vaccine preparedness for emerging pathogens? Mucosal immunity matters A clear lesson learned from the COVID-19 pandemic was that intramus­ cular vaccination can only imperfectly protect from infection with respiratory viruses per se and from onward transmission1. Vaccines that are administered via mucosal surfaces may be a better option to induce immunity in the upper respiratory tract to protect from infection with respiratory viruses. This was clearly identified as a gap, and funding agencies, including the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), set out to support the development of mucosal vaccine approaches for COVID-19 (ref. 3). Unfortunately, funding for many of these vaccines was terminated or redirected to other projects owing to the policy decision that COVID-19 is no longer a priority. How­ ever, having infection- and transmission-blocking vaccines early in an outbreak with a respiratory virus would notably increase the effect of vaccines. Although several intranasal vaccines for COVID-19 are either still in development or already licensed outside the USA and Europe4,5, there is a large gap in terms of vaccine preparedness when it comes to mucosal vaccination routes. Having mucosal vaccines with clear immunological (and potentially mucosal) correlates of protection and established vaccine efficacy and safety on the market would increase confidence in these vaccine platforms and would likely enable early deployment during an outbreak or a pandemic. Broadly protective or strain-specific vaccines Studies of influenza virus and HIV-1 have shown that RNA viruses can evolve quickly. This was also observed with SARS-CoV-2. With the emergence of the Omicron variants, vaccines had to be updated to stay effective. However, updating vaccines to respond to emerging variants means always being one step behind the virus. This is a scenario with which we are very familiar from influenza virus vaccines. Owing to the antigenic variability of RNA viruses, the development of broadly protective vaccines has been the focus in the HIV-1 and influenza fields for many years but also became an important topic for SARS-CoV-2. The concept of broadly protective vaccines goes further than the idea of covering evolving virus variants. The idea has expanded to develop vaccines that potentially can protect from whole virus families, which would considerably increase pandemic preparedness. Although fund­ ing for such vaccines has been made available (for example, via the NIAID Collaborative Influenza Vaccine Innovation Centers program, the BARDA funding initiatives and the European Health and Digital Executive Agency), they have not progressed far enough to be used in case of an emergency. Further investment is urgently needed to advance these candidates and concepts through clinical development and real­ ize their potential as tools to combat evolving viral threats and future Comment https://doi.org/10.1038/s41590-026-02726-w Check for updates Broadly protective vs virus/strain- specific vaccines Mucosal vs injected vaccines Vaccine platform Vaccine acceptance Market Regulatory policy Manufacturing speed Funding policy Basic research Vaccine preparedness Vaccine Fig. 1 | Factors and aspects that influence epidemic and pandemic vaccine preparedness. Although technology has advanced, questions about broadly protective versus specific vaccines and mucosal vaccines remain. In addition, recent changes in funding and regulatory policy increase uncertainty for vaccine preparedness. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2357–2359 | 2358 Comment pandemics. In addition, the regulatory pathway to get such vaccines licensed remains unclear. Vaccines need to be tested in phase 3 efficacy trials to show how well they protect against disease. To demonstrate that a vaccine is broadly protective, multi-year trials to show efficacy in seasons with antigenic changes are likely needed, and such trials may be prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, demonstrating efficacy against pathogens that are not yet circulating in humans is impossible, making it difficult to claim universal protection against future pathogens with pandemic potential. For pandemic preparedness, strain-matched vac­ cines that can be generated rapidly after the emergence of a new virus currently seems to be favored over the development of broadly protec­ tive vaccines (for example, https://cepi.net/100-days). Although this is of course also a good approach, it would be better to have vaccines ready before a new outbreak even starts and not months later, which is something that a broadly protective or universal vaccine could deliver. Pandemic influenza breakthroughs The recent pan-zootic with highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b influenza virus and its spillover into many mammalian species has raised concerns about the potential of this virus to cause a pandemic6. Fortunately, recent developments have enhanced pandemic influenza vaccine preparedness. For influenza vaccines, a correlate of protection accepted by regulators exists — the hemagglutination inhibition titer — although several other validated correlates of protection have also been established by academic researchers7. If a vaccine manufacturer has a licensed seasonal influenza virus vaccine on the market, the same technology can be used to manufacture a vaccine for an emerging pandemic influenza virus strain and get it to the market based on this correlate, instead of performing time-consuming phase 3 field efficacy trials first. Although effectiveness must be confirmed later, this step saves a lot of time during an outbreak. So far, this pathway has been open to manufacturers who are producing influenza vaccines using traditional technologies, such as split-inactivated vaccines. To update these vaccines to a new pandemic strain can be time-consuming. This process can be faster using the mRNA platform, but until recently, no mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccines were available, meaning that this quick strain-change pathway was not open to the mRNA technol­ ogy. The recent licensure of an mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccine from Moderna (mFLUSIVA in the USA; mCOMBRIAX in the European Union) changed this8. Although the benefits of an mRNA-based sea­ sonal influenza vaccine compared with conventional vaccines remain debated, the advantage in terms of speed in case of a pandemic is a game changer. Using the mechanism of a strain change from seasonal strains to a pandemic strain in combination with the mRNA technology may make it possible to have a matched pandemic influenza vaccine ready for use in the population within 3 months. The Bundibugyo virus outbreak as a test In May 2026, an outbreak with Bundibugyo virus was reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)9. This outbreak is still ongo­ ing, case numbers are growing and it has now become the second larg­ est outbreak of Ebola disease in recorded history. Although vaccines against another virus species, Ebola virus (formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus), are licensed and available, strain-matched vaccines for Bundibugyo virus had not been clinically developed10. This crisis in the DRC serves as test for post-COVID-19 pandemic vaccine preparedness. So far, two vaccines have moved into clinical evaluation. The first phase 1 trial, based on an adenovirus vector (ChAdOx1-BDBV-GP), began in July in the UK11. A second trial, with an mRNA vaccine, was initiated in August in Canada (mRNA-1469, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07737717). How long it takes to move these vaccines forward in the clinical pipeline, whether they are successful, and if they are fast enough to be used in the current outbreak remain to be determined. It is, however, notewor­ thy that these two vaccines are based on the same technologies that delivered the first COVID-19 vaccines. The value of basic research for vaccine preparedness Another aspect that needs to be mentioned is basic research that is being conducted to better understand emerging viruses that have so far gained little interest, especially viruses belonging to the Bunyaviri­ cetes. This class includes viruses such as severe fever with thrombocy­ topenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHVF), Toscana virus (TOSV), Heartland virus, Shamonda virus, Yezo virus12 and Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV)13, as well as hantaviruses such as Andes virus14. Some of these viruses are already human-to-human transmissible and have caused concerning outbreaks, such as the Andes virus outbreak in May on the cruise ship MV Hondius15. The spike proteins of these viruses were not well understood, making vaccine design complicated. Recent advances in understanding the molecular biology, structural biology and antigenicity of these viruses, partially funded by the excellent NIAID Research and Development of Vaccines and Monoclonal Antibodies for Pandemic Preparedness (ReVAMPP) program, have started to change that. Using new technolo­ gies and insights, vaccines against these challenging targets can now potentially also be developed quickly if needed, highlighting the need for and value of basic research. Conclusions The obvious question is, are we now, after the COVID-19 pandemic, better prepared for coming epidemics and pandemics in respect to vac­ cines? The answer is not a simple yes or no. Technology has advanced, our understanding of virus biology has markedly increased and COVID- 19 has shown us that vaccines can be developed quickly if needed and if an effort is made by all stakeholders. However, there is much still to learn; from basic research and clinical testing to manufacturing and regulatory policies. Importantly, funding policies and regulatory policies are changing in parts of the world, partially influenced by the anti-vaccine movement that now has advocates within governments. It is unclear what the long-term effect of these changes is on vaccine development and pandemic preparedness. title_original: Vaccine preparedness for the next emerging infectious disease crisis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for improved vaccine preparedness against emerging infectious diseases, highlighting the lessons learned from the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and the ongoing challenges in developing effective vaccines for future threats.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a commentary analyzing current vaccine preparedness strategies, focusing on the development of mucosal vaccines and broadly protective vaccines for emerging pathogens, with an emphasis on avian influenza A viruses.
analysis.methods: The methods involve a review of existing vaccine technologies, regulatory frameworks, and recent developments in basic research, including the role of programs like ReVAMPP in advancing understanding of emerging viruses.
analysis.main_results: The results indicate that while mRNA-based vaccines offer faster development during pandemics, there remains a significant gap in mucosal vaccine preparedness. Additionally, the study notes that the regulatory pathway for licensing such vaccines is still unclear.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the current focus on strain-matched vaccines, rather than broadly protective ones, may limit long-term pandemic preparedness. They highlight the novelty of considering mucosal immunity as a key factor in vaccine development.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that investing in mucosal vaccine platforms and broadly protective vaccines could enhance preparedness for future outbreaks, particularly those involving avian influenza A viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a commentary and does not include direct experimental results, which limits its strength. The confidence in the conclusions is moderate due to the reliance on existing literature and policy discussions.

analysis.summary_en: This commentary evaluates the current state of vaccine preparedness for emerging infectious diseases, particularly avian influenza A viruses. It highlights the importance of mucosal immunity and the need for broadly protective vaccines, while noting the challenges in regulatory pathways and funding. The study emphasizes that although mRNA technology has accelerated vaccine development, there remains a gap in mucosal vaccine strategies. It also discusses the role of basic research in improving preparedness and the impact of policy decisions on vaccine development. The findings suggest that future efforts should prioritize mucosal vaccine platforms and broader protection strategies to better respond to evolving viral threats. However, the commentary lacks direct experimental results, which limits the strength of its conclusions.

elements_zh.main_results: 结果表明,虽然基于 mRNA 的 疫苗 在大流行期间提供更快的发育,但粘膜 疫苗 的准备仍然存在显着差距。此外,研究指出,疫苗 等许可的监管途径仍不清楚。

full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2363 The European Vaccines Hub Rino Rappuoli, Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding, Pierre Van Damme, James P. Di Santo, Donata Medaglini & Michel Pletschette The European Vaccines Hub is a novel design consortium that assembles leading European organizations involved in vaccine development. The mission is to develop vaccines and monoclonal antibodies ensuring Europe’s pandemics and emerging infections readiness. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the European Union, it was insufficiently prepared to face the devastating health and economic emergency. Although European biotech contributed significantly to the development of vaccines with products such as Comirnaty, the mRNA vaccine developed by the German BioNTech was eventually licensed to and commercialized by an American company, meaning that very few European medical countermeasures reached the market at the peak of the pandemic. A further weakness identified was that Europe did not partici- pate in any of the pivotal efficacy trials leading to licensure. To address this situation, the European Commission established the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA) as one of its Directorates General, with the mission of strengthening the European Union’s ability to respond to major health threats through coordination, expertise and the development and procurement of medical countermeasures (MCMs). In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, HERA published a call for proposals for the creation of a European Hub for vaccine development, with the mission of developing, assessing and manufacturing vaccines for priority pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential to ensure that Europe would be more resilient through increased preparedness. This new entity was designed to be not another institution, but rather a newly created network of existing organizations already funded by their member states to develop vaccines. The mandate of the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) was to create a hub able to develop and deliver vaccines end-to-end, from discovery to manufacturing. To achieve this, the EVH was expected to be organ- ized in an agile manner, allowing it to make quick decisions and to include and engage with any group from industry, biotech or academia that could contribute to development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against pathogens with pandemic risk. Unique new structure The EVH consortium selected for funding enabled the creation of an innovative organization that has the expertise and facilities to provide the European Union with self-sustainable and independent ability to discover, develop, assess and manufacture vaccines and antibodies against infectious diseases of epidemic and pandemic potential. This organization is based on four pillars (Fig. 1). Pillar 1 leads vaccines and monoclonal antibody discovery while advancing platforms to develop vaccines based on protein and adjuvants, on mRNA or on viral vectors. Pillar 2 drives preclinical studies to support the discovery, charac- terization and development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. Pillar 3 coordinates clinical development, which includes the readiness to perform ad hoc phase 1 and 2 studies and controlled human challenge studies (CHIM), with the overarching goals of putting together a network of European vaccine clinical trial centers under consented protocols and preparing to conduct large-scale phase 3 studies in collaboration with the EU ‘BE READY NOW’ project. In pillar 4, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Center for Pandemic Vaccines and Therapeutics (ZEPAI) oversee regulatory coordination and planning of manufacturing of small-scale Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) lots for early clinical studies, as well as large-scale manufacturing of final products. Although the primary scope of the EVH is to develop and build the capacity to deliver medical countermeasures, it is designed as an open organization that reaches out and engages with small and large vaccine manufacturers, biotech, academic groups, R&D units of pharmaceuti- cal companies, and projects and networks funded by European Union, for example through the Horizon Europe program. To achieve this, the EVH is following two noteworthy paths: the creation of an innovative public–private partnership model with industry and the promotion of ‘expression of interest’ calls for experts and specific projects, enabling the EVH to liaise with experts and collaborating centers that share a similar mission, both within and outside the European Union. The arrows below each pillar in Fig. 1 denote the continuous interchange between the EVH and the European system. Projects Priority projects for the EVH are developments that tackle infec- tious diseases with epidemic and pandemic potential relevant to the European Union. Projects are proposed by the EVH and agreed upon Comment https://doi.org/10.1038/s41590-026-02653-w Check for updates Discovery of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies Novel technology platforms for vaccine and antibody development Biotecnopolo Siena, Italy Preclinical assessment of vaccine and antibody prototypes Institut Pasteur Paris, France Preclinical studies Coordination of ambulatory clinical trials, CHIM and immunological analyses Vaccinopolis University of Antwerp, Belgium Clinical studies Reliable and well-prepared European pandemic manufacturing capacities and regulatory preparedness DZIF ZEPAI, Germany Manufacturing and regulatory Platform infrastructures EVH activities Vaccines and antibodies manufacturing plan EVH European ecosystem Pillar 1 Pillar 2 Pillar 3 Pillar 4 Fig. 1 | Schematic representation of the organization and function of the European Vaccines Hub. The organization’s base is the entirety of Europe, and it is organized in four pillars that comprise the activities necessary for end-to-end vaccine delivery. The arrows below each pillar indicate that any European entity can take or bring projects. CHIM, controlled human challenge studies. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2364 Comment with HERA. The initial priority pathogens identified were avian influ- enza, in particular H5N1, and monkeypox (mpox). EVH activities include building the preparedness system and testing it. Indeed, the EVH’s mission creates a system that allows continuous delivery and regular updates for priorities. A living EU Epidemic and Pandemic Vaccine Readiness Plan agreed to with HERA generates an agile basis for EU pandemic preparedness. One year after the EVH was established, each of the four pillars has initiated a variety of projects and delivered important results. Pillar 1 discovered a potent and broadly protective monoclonal anti- body against mpox that recognizes a vaccine antigen not previously known to induce neutralizing antibodies. In vivo and in vitro studies in collaboration with pillar 2 confirmed that the mpox monoclonal antibody and the vaccine antigen are protective in vivo and are good candidates for continued MCM development. Pillar 3 has designed and fully enrolled a clinical trial to study the vaccine response of the European population to primary and booster immunization against the avian influenza H5N1, and is currently assessing its outcome. In the trial, H5N1-naive participants and participants immunized in 2006 with a H5N1 vaccine received an adjuvanted vaccine against the current Astrakhan clade. The study has the additional scope to establish a study cohort whose peripheral blood cells can be used to discover broadly neutralizing antibodies that recognize epitopes shared between the 2006 and 2026 H5N1 strains. Pillar 4 is addressing important bottlenecks in preparedness by mapping the European GMP facilities ready to manufacture vaccines and monoclonals for small-scale clinical trials and developing concepts for rapid ramp-up to large-scale manufacturing in pandemic crises. Its regulatory experts are addressing the anticipated practical and scientific regulatory questions required for accelerating development of EVH products to enable early availability of products. In addition, the EVH has initiated collaborations with external entities. One involves joint participation with Sanofi, a major Euro- pean vaccine manufacturer, in an EU tender to develop a mucosal mRNA vaccine against the H5N1 avian influenza. Another involves the publication of an ‘expression of interest’ to identify possible col- laborators that can contribute to further pandemic influenza vaccine development approaches. Stress testing While the EVH was working on setting up its organization, two unex- pected, highly lethal emerging infections were communicated by the World Health Organization in May 2026. The first was the Andes hanta- virus outbreak, reported on 2 May, involving a cruise ship coming out of Argentina1, and the second was the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda that was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May2. Although these were not imminent threats for Europe, after rapid consultation with HERA, it was agreed that it would be important for Europe to par- ticipate in the development of countermeasures for these viruses. The question was whether the EVH had the capacity to address these two targets that, up to that moment, had never been considered. Consultation of the EVH network identified a broadly protective human monoclonal antibody against Andes hantavirus discovered in a Swedish patient infected with Puumala hantavirus, which had been characterized by several German academic groups and whose structure had been determined a few years ago at the Institut Pasteur in Paris3. This antibody had been acquired and improved by two US R&D enterprises but was never brought into clinical development. Concurrently, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) labora- tories revealed recent results identifying a potent human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes both Ebola Zaire and Ebola Bundibugyo. The antibody had been shown to protect mice from challenge with the virus in the Biosafety Level 4 (BSL4) facility in Marburg4. As such, in less than a month, the two antibodies were selected by the EVH for development up to clinical testing. For antibody expression, EVH is developing an innovative platform based on the C1 fungus, which is expected to enable cost-effective production of large quantities of monoclonal antibodies, making these therapies more accessible to at-risk populations and to low-income countries at an affordable and equitable cost5. The stress test arising from the unexpected outbreaks showed that the EVH can leverage the ad hoc development of a multitude of innova- tive prototypes from excellent European entities that have hitherto failed to translate them into products when working in isolation. The EVH can turn these product candidates into countermeasures to protect people’s health. Moreover, the EVH network had at its disposal two vac- cine prototypes for the development of an Ebola vaccine: an MVA-based vaccine against Ebola Zaire developed by DZIF-associated EVH mem- bers, previously shown to be protective in a mouse challenge study performed at the Marburg BSL-4 facility6, and a measles vector-based pan-filovirus vaccine in development at the Institut Pasteur. Once added to the EVH portfolio, these projects could become highly relevant in the race against Bundibugyo virus. Furthermore, monoclonal antibodies candidates could provide an important complementary strategy, with the advantage of providing immediate protection. Looking to the future In conclusion, the EVH is an organization rooting pandemic prepar- edness within an innovative cross-sectorial ecosystem, which in its first year of existence has shown the potential to deliver innovative countermeasures. We can probably describe the EVH as both a dis- covery and development engine and a catalyst able to aggregate the best European competencies and discoveries, transforming them into medical products that include vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. The big question is whether the EVH will be able to exploit this poten- tial and deliver real products. There are numerous challenges that could interfere with this ambitious goal. One of the most important limitations is the fact that the products in the EVH portfolio do not have an immediate attractive commercial market value because they address infectious diseases that are rare, or pandemics that we hope will never happen. The absence of immediate commercial value, com- monly defined as a market failure, is a recurrent problem for most medical countermeasures. In the absence of an expected immediate and secure return on investment, the private sector is little inclined to start rapid development and manufacturing programs. Notwithstand- ing that complication, the instruments developed by the EU in terms of stockpiling essential and possibly innovative MCMs and the constant readiness of the reality-tested joint procurement mechanism are robust attempts to provide solutions to these problems. Although we have the technology to develop effective products against most infectious diseases, these need to become available for wide implementation despite the absence of immediate pre- dictable markets. It is therefore important to address, on a global scale, the longer-term sustainability of MCM development, which can be clearly seen to be an insurance for the health and economic security of every country, and to move out of the disastrous cycle of panic and neglect. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2365 Comment Rino Rappuoli 1,2 , Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding1,3,4, Pierre Van Damme 1,5, James P. Di Santo, Donata Medaglini & Michel Pletschette The European Vaccines Hub is a novel design consortium that assembles leading European organizations involved in vaccine development. The mission is to develop vaccines and monoclonal antibodies ensuring Europe’s pandemics and emerging infections readiness. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the European Union, it was insufficiently prepared to face the devastating health and economic emergency. Although European biotech contributed significantly to the development of vaccines with products such as Comirnaty, the mRNA vaccine developed by the German BioNTech was eventually licensed to and commercialized by an American company, meaning that very few European medical countermeasures reached the market at the peak of the pandemic. A further weakness identified was that Europe did not partici- pate in any of the pivotal efficacy trials leading to licensure. To address this situation, the European Commission established the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA) as one of its Directorates General, with the mission of strengthening the European Union’s ability to respond to major health threats through coordination, expertise and the development and procurement of medical countermeasures (MCMs). In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, HERA published a call for proposals for the creation of a European Hub for vaccine development, with the mission of developing, assessing and manufacturing vaccines for priority pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential to ensure that Europe would be more resilient through increased preparedness. This new entity was designed to be not another institution, but rather a newly created network of existing organizations already funded by their member states to develop vaccines. The mandate of the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) was to create a hub able to develop and deliver vaccines end-to-end, from discovery to manufacturing. To achieve this, the EVH was expected to be organ- ized in an agile manner, allowing it to make quick decisions and to include and engage with any group from industry, biotech or academia that could contribute to development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against pathogens with pandemic risk. Unique new structure The EVH consortium selected for funding enabled the creation of an innovative organization that has the expertise and facilities to provide the European Union with self-sustainable and independent ability to discover, develop, assess and manufacture vaccines and antibodies against infectious diseases of epidemic and pandemic potential. This organization is based on four pillars (Fig. 1). Pillar 1 leads vaccines and monoclonal antibody discovery while advancing platforms to develop vaccines based on protein and adjuvants, on mRNA or on viral vectors. Pillar 2 drives preclinical studies to support the discovery, charac- terization and development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. Pillar 3 coordinates clinical development, which includes the readiness to perform ad hoc phase 1 and 2 studies and controlled human challenge studies (CHIM), with the overarching goals of putting together a network of European vaccine clinical trial centers under consented protocols and preparing to conduct large-scale phase 3 studies in collaboration with the EU ‘BE READY NOW’ project. In pillar 4, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Center for Pandemic Vaccines and Therapeutics (ZEPAI) oversee regulatory coordination and planning of manufacturing of small-scale Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) lots for early clinical studies, as well as large-scale manufacturing of final products. Although the primary scope of the EVH is to develop and build the capacity to deliver medical countermeasures, it is designed as an open organization that reaches out and engages with small and large vaccine manufacturers, biotech, academic groups, R&D units of pharmaceuti- cal companies, and projects and networks funded by European Union, for example through the Horizon Europe program. To achieve this, the EVH is following two noteworthy paths: the creation of an innovative public–private partnership model with industry and the promotion of ‘expression of interest’ calls for experts and specific projects, enabling the EVH to liaise with experts and collaborating centers that share a similar mission, both within and outside the European Union. The arrows below each pillar in Fig. 1 denote the continuous interchange between the EVH and the European system. Indeed, the EVH’s mission creates a system that allows continuous delivery and regular updates for priorities. A living EU Epidemic and Pandemic Vaccine Readiness Plan agreed to with HERA generates an agile basis for EU pandemic preparedness. One year after the EVH was established, each of the four pillars has initiated a variety of projects and delivered important results. Pillar 1 discovered a potent and broadly protective monoclonal anti- body against mpox that recognizes a vaccine antigen not previously known to induce neutralizing antibodies. In vivo and in vitro studies in collaboration with pillar 2 confirmed that the mpox monoclonal antibody and the vaccine antigen are protective in vivo and are good candidates for continued MCM development. Pillar 3 has designed and fully enrolled a clinical trial to study the vaccine response of the European population to primary and booster immunization against the avian influenza H5N1, and is currently assessing its outcome. title_original: The European Vaccines Hub

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the European Union’s lack of preparedness for pandemics and emerging infections, particularly highlighting the need for a coordinated system to develop and deliver vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against priority pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes the establishment of the European Vaccines Hub (EVH) as a network of existing organizations funded by member states, designed to create an agile system for vaccine development, clinical trials, and manufacturing readiness across Europe.
analysis.methods: The EVH employs a public–private partnership model, coordinates clinical development through ad hoc phase 1 and 2 studies, and prepares for large-scale phase 3 trials. It also maps European GMP facilities for vaccine manufacturing and develops concepts for rapid scaling during pandemics.
analysis.main_results: The EVH has conducted a clinical trial to assess the vaccine response of the European population to primary and booster immunization against avian influenza H5N1 and is currently evaluating its outcomes. Additionally, it has identified a potent human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes both Ebola Zaire and Ebola Bundibugyo strains.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the EVH has demonstrated the potential to deliver innovative countermeasures by leveraging ad hoc development of prototypes from European entities, showcasing its agility and effectiveness in pandemic preparedness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of a resilient European pandemic preparedness system, emphasizing the importance of a coordinated network for vaccine development, clinical trials, and manufacturing, which can be applied to other priority pathogens with epidemic potential.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on the design and initial activities of the EVH, with a moderate confidence level due to the absence of detailed results and the reliance on planned rather than completed studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study outlines the establishment of the European Vaccines Hub (EVH) as a coordinated network of European organizations aimed at improving pandemic preparedness. The EVH was created in response to the EU's insufficient readiness during the COVID-19 pandemic, with a focus on developing vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against priority pathogens like avian influenza H5N1. The EVH employs an agile public–private partnership model, coordinates clinical trials, and maps manufacturing capacities to ensure rapid response during health emergencies. The first results include a clinical trial assessing vaccine response against H5N1 and the identification of a monoclonal antibody effective against multiple Ebola strains. The authors interpret these findings as demonstrating the EVH's potential to deliver innovative countermeasures. The study highlights the importance of a unified system for vaccine development and manufacturing, which can be applied to other epidemic threats. However, the evidence is based on planned activities rather than completed results, limiting the confidence in its current effectiveness.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决欧盟对流行病和新出现的感染缺乏准备的问题,特别强调需要一个协调的系统来开发和提供 疫苗 和针对具有流行和大流行潜力的优先病原体的单克隆抗体。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究描述了欧洲 疫苗 中心 (EVH) 的建立,作为由成员国资助的现有组织网络,旨在为整个欧洲的 疫苗 开发、临床试验和制造准备创建一个敏捷系统。
elements_zh.methods: EVH 采用公私合作模式,通过临时 1 期和 2 期研究协调临床开发,并为大规模 3 期试验做好准备。它还绘制了 疫苗 制造的欧洲 GMP 设施图,并开发了在大流行期间快速扩展的概念。
elements_zh.main_results: EVH 进行了一项临床试验,以评估欧洲人群对 禽流感 H5N1 初次免疫和加强免疫的 疫苗 反应,目前正在评估其结果。此外,它还发现了一种有效的人类单克隆抗体,可以中和扎伊尔埃博拉病毒株和本迪布焦埃博拉病毒株。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,EVH 已经证明了通过利用欧洲实体原型的临时开发来提供创新对策的潜力,展示了其在大流行病防范方面的敏捷性和有效性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为欧洲大流行病应对系统的发展提供了信息,强调了 疫苗 开发、临床试验和制造协调网络的重要性,该网络可应用于其他具有流行潜力的优先病原体。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于 EVH 的设计和初始活动,由于缺乏详细结果以及依赖计划研究而不是已完成的研究,因此具有中等置信度。

full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2355 | 2355 Vaccinology 2.0 The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the success of vaccine development, but more improvements in vaccine design, equity, manufacturing and changes in public health policy are warranted. O ne of the global health success stories has been the develop­ ment of vaccines. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), we now have vaccines to more than 30 life-threatening infections, which is estimated to prevent 3.5 million to 5 million deaths every year. The recent COVID-19 pandemic showcased vaccine development at its best. Vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed, facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform and spurred by the wealth of existing knowledge of virology, vac­ cinology and structural biology. However, much has changed since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. In this issue of Nature Immunology, we have commissioned several commentaries from experts across the globe that collectively summarize recent progress and discuss the challenges faced in this field. Although the COVID-19 pandemic high­ lighted the transformative potential of mRNA platforms, gaps remain for global pandemic preparedness according to Florian Kram­ mer. In his Comment, Krammer argues that there is a need to advance mucosal vaccines to improve protection against respiratory infection and transmission, and to develop more broadly protective vaccines that target entire virus families. In addition, strengthen­ ing regulatory policy and sustaining support for basic research on emerging pathogens is needed. However, the current US adminis­ tration has adopted measures that weaken vaccine development in the USA by the deci­ sion to withdraw federal support for mRNA vaccine development. This action led to the cancellation of research grant contracts worth approximately US$500 million, affecting ongoing mRNA therapeutic projects involv­ ing universities, research institutes and major pharmaceutical companies. In addition to funding cuts, the public health policies of the current US government are promoting vaccine hesitancy. In a World View article, Peter Hotez argues that the rise of the US Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has weakened confidence in evidence-based medicine, contributed to out­ breaks of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, and fostered efforts to replace established scientific and regulatory frame­ works with wellness-oriented ideologies. Wor­ ryingly, vaccine hesitancy has evolved from a movement focused on COVID-19 vaccines into a broader anti-science campaign that increas­ ingly shapes public health policy, promotes misinformation and extends to areas such as childhood immunization, autism, fluoride, raw milk and alternative medicine. Further­ more, Hotez warns that these trends are spreading internationally, particularly into Europe, raising concerns that growing accept­ ance of pseudoscientific health policies could undermine pandemic preparedness, biomedi­ cal research and public health outcomes on a global scale. On a more optimistic note, in their Com­ ment Michael J. Hogan and Norbert Pardi discuss advances across other RNA technolo­ gies that aim to improve efficacy, reduce reac­ togenicity and enhance T cell and mucosal immune responses. A deeper understanding of RNA and lipid-nanoparticle biology, com­ bined with innovations in delivery systems and immune modulation, is still needed to engi­ neer vaccines that produce different types of immune response depending on the disease being treated. Similarly, the COVID-19 pan­ demic exposed the vulnerability of Africa and other lower-income regions to dependence on external vaccine suppliers. Shabir A. Madhi and Glenda E. Gray state in their Comment that the local manufacturing of routine vaccines in Africa is often economically uncompeti­ tive and may divert resources from broader public health goals. Instead, they advocate for strategic investment in adaptable vaccine platforms such as mRNA and viral-vector technologies, outbreak-response manufac­ turing capacity, regulatory expertise, clini­ cal development infrastructure and skilled workforce development. In their Comment, Rino Rappuoli et al. high­ light the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) created in response to short­ comings exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The EVH is designed to strengthen pandemic preparedness by integrating vaccine and monoclonal antibody discovery, preclinical and clinical development, regulatory plan­ ning and manufacturing capabilities into a coordinated, end-to-end development net­ work. The initiative aims to translate Europe’s strong scientific base into deployable medi­ cal countermeasures for emerging infectious diseases and is currently focusing on threats such as H5N1 influenza. The authors highlight EVH’s early achievements, including the iden­ tification of promising vaccine and antibody candidates, the establishment of clinical trial infrastructure, and rapid responses to emerging threats, such as Andes hantavirus and Ebola Bundibugyo outbreaks. Finally, in his Comment, Bali Pulendran looks at the future of vaccine research by pointing out the vaccine-induced protection extends beyond antibody and T cell responses to encompass a broader spectrum of ‘protec­ tive immune states’ within tissues, in which coordinated networks of immune and non­ immune cells confer heightened resistance to infection. Recent studies of intravenous BCG and mucosal vaccination suggest that protection can emerge from coordinated interactions among adaptive immune cells, innate cells and structural cells within tissues. These interactions create organ-embedded states of increased resistance that provide broad protection against diverse pathogens, a phenomenon termed ‘integrated organ immu­ nity’. Pulendran proposes that future vacci­ nology should shift from focusing primarily on antigens and immune correlates toward identifying, characterizing and deliberately engineering these protective immune states, potentially enabling more durable and broadly protective vaccines against infectious diseases and other immune-mediated conditions. This ‘Vaccinology 2.0’ focus highlights the achievements of vaccine research in the past 6 years and showcases issues that still need to be tackled to ensure the continued development, improvement and accessibility of vaccines for future generations and ensure that we are prepared for the next pandemic. Published online: 23 November 2026 Editorial https://doi.org/10.1038/s41590-026-02725-x Check for updates
